idea: Halftone of Earthrise (NASA, Apollo 8, 1968), the grey Moon horizon with the small Earth above it, caption: 'The first time anyone saw the whole thing from outside.' Printed white on black; for people who want one quiet picture that changes the scale of everything.
NASA's 'Blue Marble' / early ATS-3 full-disc Earth halftone, caption: 'No borders were visible. Several were checked.' A dry geography joke for people who know the map is an agreement, not a feature.

Library of Congress photograph of a 1870s Wheeler Survey party at camp in the desert, with a theodolite on a tripod, caption: 'Somebody had to go and stand there first.' For the person who respects fieldwork over armchair opinions.

Timothy O'Sullivan's survey photograph of the wagon darkroom in the Nevada desert (public domain), caption: 'Mobile darkroom. Nearest water: 40 miles.' A tribute to people who carried absurd equipment to get one true image.

Frank Hurley's Endurance, trapped and lit by flares in the Weddell Sea ice (1915), halftone with the caption: 'Plan B was also a boat.' For anyone who values improvising when the original plan froze solid.
Amundsen's party at the South Pole tent with the Norwegian flag (1911), caption: 'Arrived. Left a note. Went home early.' A wry salute to competence without drama.

Close halftone of a brass sextant and chronometer from a public-domain museum photo, caption: 'Where am I? A fair question, answered by arithmetic and the sky.' A beautiful object with a point of view: navigation was once pure thinking.

Early aerial photograph of Boston taken from a balloon by James Wallace Black (1860), caption: 'The first view of a city from above. It looked smaller.' For people who love the moment a place first saw itself from outside.

1946 V-2 rocket photograph of Earth from 65 miles up (White Sands, public domain), grainy halftone, caption: 'Taken by a camera that did not expect to survive.' Referencing the film cassette that was recovered from the wreckage, for lovers of gutsy first pictures.

Photograph of a lone USGS surveyor holding a stadia rod on a ridge, the vast Grand Canyon behind him, caption: 'Benchmark.' A one-word shirt for those who like to be a fixed point others measure from.
Ice-covered Arctic ship (Fram or Karluk archive photo) with rigging frozen white, caption: 'Drifted three years on purpose.' For people who understand that some strategies are patience.
Gertrude Bell or an early woman explorer on camelback in the desert, Library of Congress halftone, caption: 'Went anyway.' A short, confident shirt for people who need no permission slip.
Halftone of Apollo 17 astronaut's boot print on lunar regolith or Aldrin's Apollo 11 footprint, caption: 'Still there. No wind.' A calm, smart observation about permanence for space nerds.

NASA Landsat or Apollo-era photograph of the Nile delta, a green fan in desert, caption: 'Egypt, seen from where you can see it is a river.' For geography people who love when scale reveals the logic.
Library of Congress photograph of a ship's compass binnacle glowing at night, caption: 'Magnetic north is moving. Keep adjusting.' A gentle life lesson built on a real scientific fact.

Photograph of a Polynesian-style stick chart is not photo-safe, so instead a Smithsonian/Library photo of a ship's compass binnacle at night, caption: 'Magnetic north is moving. Keep adjusting.' A gentle life lesson with a real scientific fact.
The 1890s USGS survey party lined up with their pack mules on a mountain trail, caption: 'The mules had better maps than the committee.' A wry shirt for anyone who trusts the ground over the office.
Public-domain NASA photo of the Himalaya or Alps taken from the Space Shuttle, halftoned, caption: 'The mountain does not know it has a name.' A humble, poetic one for the map-obsessed.

Library of Congress photograph of an early 1920s aerial mapping camera mounted in a biplane, caption: 'Everything below is a measurement.' For cartography fans who like seeing how maps were really made.

Lighthouse at night in a 1900s Library of Congress Detroit Publishing halftone, beam cutting across fog, caption: 'It has one job and does it.' A warm, minimal shirt about reliability for people tired of hustle culture.
